Core UX concepts

The signature idea: Google's four colours are the four mastery dimensions from the architecture doc, and each concept is a ring that fills one colour at a time.

ColourDimensionStudent-facing meaningFilled by
BlueConcept"I understand it"Lesson checks, answers in any language
RedTechnical words"I know what it's called"Word stickers, term matching
YellowAcademic English"I can explain it in English"English questions, Teach Kiki
GreenPractical"I can make it work"Lab tasks, debugging

A right answer in Odia with a weak English answer keeps Blue full and lowers only Yellow. The screen says so: "You understand this. You just need the English words for it."

Supporting mechanics:

  • Concept map as a circuit board. Concepts are components, prerequisites are wires. Mastery sends current to the next node. It works as a metaphor for all three branches: signals, power and process flows.
  • Route to Mid-sem. A Google Maps-style blue route through the map, weighted by past papers, with an ETA. A wrong answer triggers "Rerouting…" through a missing prerequisite.
  • Language dial. Odia-to-English slider on every lesson. Student-controlled. Kiki suggests a step toward English after a run of correct answers.
  • Word stickers. Collectible term cards (English term, Odia meaning, audio, mini diagram, example sentence). Reused as drag-in chips when writing English answers.
  • Draw your prediction. The student sketches the expected waveform or curve before running a simulation. The real output is overlaid on the sketch.
  • Detective debug. A deliberately broken setup. Kiki asks "why" questions before giving any hint.
  • Teach Kiki. The student explains the concept to Kiki in English, by voice or text. Kiki plays a confused junior.
  • Flickering nodes. Mastered nodes dim over days. A short revisit with less help relights them (spaced revision).
  • Kiki's form. Four Google-coloured dots that bounce while thinking, become an arrow to point, form a "?" to ask, and burst on success.

Onboarding, end to end

Onboarding is one continuous story: a link arrives in a WhatsApp group, the student learns one concept in 10 minutes, and the session closes with proof they learned it plus a card they can share. Setup questions come after the first win, not before it.

We tell it through one fictional student, used in the demo too:

  • Bikash, first semester, Electronics and Communication, at an engineering college in Odisha.
  • Studied in Odia medium through Class 12.
  • Basic Electronics mid-sem in 12 days. A diode rectifier lab next week.
  • Has an Android phone with patchy data. Uses the college lab laptop for practicals.

Whichever way they come in, students go through the same first open, session and close. The share card at the end is how the next student arrives.

Step 1: How the link reaches them

Every way in is a smart link. It carries the student's class context, so they land on something useful with their details already filled in. Nothing to install: it opens in the phone's browser.

What a smart link carries:

PartExampleWhat it does for the student
DestinationA concept, a mid-sem route, a lab walkthrough, a word stickerDecides where they land
Class codeCollege, branch, semester, sectionPre-fills the syllabus and mid-sem date, and shows "38 classmates are on this route"
ReferrerThe classmate who shared itThe first screen says "Shared by Rohan"

The domain is to be decided, since there is no product name yet. Shape: <domain>/route/basic-electronics?class=<code>&ref=<id>.

The ways a link gets to Bikash:

ChannelWho shares itWhat they shareWhere it lands
WhatsApp class groupClass representative, before mid-sem"Basic Electronics mid-sem route"The route, with the first stop open
WhatsApp, from a classmateAny student, at the end of their session"I can explain diodes in English" cardThat concept's mini-lesson
Class QR codeProfessor, on a slide in the first weekClass codeThe branch map with the class pre-filled
Lab QR codeLab instructor, printed on the experiment sheetThat experimentOn a phone: a 5-minute warm-up. On a laptop: Kiki's lab walkthrough

What the WhatsApp message looks like:

  • A rich preview card. WhatsApp shows the link's preview image and title. The image has Kiki's four dots, the concept name in English with an Odia subtitle, and "10 min · Odia + English".
  • A pre-written message in mixed Odia and English. The sharer can edit it before sending.

How the first links get into groups:

  • For a real launch, we recruit one faculty champion and the class representatives in each section. Before each exam they get a ready-made mid-sem route link. Lab instructors get printable QR sheets, one per experiment.
  • For the hackathon demo, we open on a mock WhatsApp class group. The class representative's message and preview card are on screen, and we tap it.

Phone-to-laptop handoff for labs works like WhatsApp Web. The lab laptop opens a short address and shows a QR code. Bikash scans it with the phone, which is already signed in, and the laptop session joins their account.

Step 2: First open, the first 60 seconds

Bikash taps the class representative's link. Within 60 seconds there is a greeting from Kiki, a clear promise of what the next 10 minutes will achieve, a language choice, and one "before" question. There is no sign-up, no form and no install prompt.

  1. Kiki arrives (0 to 2 s). Kiki's four dots bounce in and join up while the page loads. The page is kept light so it loads on slow data.
  2. "Tap to hear Kiki" (2 to 10 s). Browsers block sound until the user taps, so the first tap is the greeting. Kiki speaks in Odia, with the words on screen: "Namaskar! I'm Kiki. Rohan shared your Basic Electronics mid-sem route." Under it: "Shared by Rohan · 38 classmates on this route".
  3. The promise (10 to 30 s). A route preview: "Mid-sem in 12 days · 9 stops · First stop: Diode, 10 min". Under it, today's goal as a can-do sentence: "In 10 minutes you'll be able to explain in English why a diode lets current flow only one way." A big blue Start button, and a small "Show me the whole map" link.
  4. "Which feels easy?" (30 to 50 s). One Class 12 sentence about electric current, shown three ways: mostly Odia, mixed, mostly English. Bikash taps one and the dial is set. Kiki points to the dial: "You can change this any time."
  5. The "before" question (50 to 60 s). Kiki: "What do you think right now? No marks." One question on today's goal, in English, with "I don't know yet" as a valid answer. Kiki cheers whichever they pick. This answer is saved for the before-and-after at the end of the session.

What the class code saved: college, branch, semester, syllabus and mid-sem date are already known, so Bikash never sees those questions.

Step 3: The first session

The first session is one concept in about 10 minutes: the diode as a one-way gate, which builds on Class 12 semiconductors. A progress bar along the top shows the four ring colours filling as Bikash goes.

BeatTimeWhat Bikash doesWhat fills
1. Hook30 sSees a phone charger and hears Kiki in Odia: "The socket gives AC, but your phone needs DC. Who decides which way current flows?"Nothing yet
2. Learn3 minShort explanation at the dial position, with forward bias, reverse bias and cut-in voltage as tappable English chips. Drags a voltage slider and watches current flow one way only, with the V-I curve drawing live. Two quick check questions.Blue
3. Collect1 minGets three word stickers (forward bias, reverse bias, cut-in voltage), hears each one pronounced, and matches each to its picture.Red, partly
4. Try it in English2 minAnswers in English: "Why does a reverse-biased diode not conduct?" Can drag stickers into the answer. If wrong, Kiki diagnoses concept or language and reroutes.Yellow, partly
5. Say it1 minRecords one English sentence by voice: "A diode conducts when…". Kiki plays it back and points out one word to improve.Yellow
6. Lab tease30 sSees the locked green segment: "Build a half-wave rectifier in Tuesday's lab to complete this ring." Kiki offers a Monday-night reminder.Green stays locked

Beat 5 matters. Hearing your own voice explain an engineering idea in English is the moment we want Bikash to remember, and it feeds directly into the close.

Step 4: Closing the session

The close proves learning with evidence, not praise. Bikash sees what they could not do 10 minutes ago and can do now, hears their own English, and leaves with one booked next step. It takes about 90 seconds.

  1. Before and after. Kiki brings back the "before" question, side by side: "10 minutes ago: I don't know yet. Now: correct, in English." This is the core proof.
  2. Your voice. Kiki replays the English sentence from beat 5: "You said this, in English."
  3. The ring. Blue, Red and Yellow fill in turn. The Green outline pulses, locked until the lab.
  4. The map reveal. The view zooms out to the whole route for the first time. The Diode node lights up, current flows to the next node, and the counter drops from "9 stops" to "8 stops". The full map is a reward here, not a setup screen.
  5. Words learned. "3 new English words." If the dial moved toward English during the session, Kiki shows that too.
  6. Save it. "Sign in with Google to keep your ring and route." The account ask comes now because there is something to lose. If they skip, progress stays on this phone.
  7. Share (optional). An "I can explain diodes in English" card showing their ring, with a pre-written WhatsApp message. This is what brings the next student in.
  8. One next step. Specific and timed: "Next stop: Diode as a rectifier, 12 min", or "Tuesday lab. 5-minute warm-up on Monday at 8 pm?" with a Remind me button.
  9. Goodbye. Kiki's dots burst in four colours, with one line in Odia.

When the session goes badly, the close stays honest. "Today you found a gap: current and voltage basics from Class 12. That's what today was for." The ring shows only what the evidence supports, and the reroute appears as progress: "1 stop added, 6 min". Rings are never filled to make someone feel good.

A good session, in measurable terms, has three parts:

  • The can-do goal is met: the "after" answer is correct in English.
  • At least one ring colour moved forward.
  • A next step is booked, either a reminder or a next stop.

Arriving without a link

A student who finds the product directly, with no class code, adds only two short taps before the same first session. Everything else waits until after the first win.

  1. Kiki greets, then "Which feels easy?" (same as Step 2).
  2. About me: chips for college, branch and semester. For the demo, only Electronics is active and the other branches say "coming soon".
  3. What do you need? "Mid-sem is coming", "Lab is confusing", "I'm lost in class" or "Get interview-ready". This picks the first node.
  4. The "before" question, then the same 10-minute session and close (Steps 3 and 4).
  5. After the close: "Make your route exact. Snap your syllabus or past papers." Gemini reads them, past-paper weights adjust the route, and they can pop the English words they already know to fill their sticker deck.

How students use it day to day

Home is the map, not a feed. Most sessions are one tap on a big "Continue with Kiki" button, which runs the Learning Orchestrator's next step. A goal card sits above the map: "Mid-sem in 12 days. 3 stops left."

A concept gap sends the student back through a prerequisite. A language gap sends them to word stickers and an easier English version. Only answers solid on both move on to the lab.

ModeDeviceHow they enterWhat Kiki doesColours it fills
LearnPhoneContinue, or tap a nodeExplains at the dial position, checks understanding, diagnosesBlue, Red
ExamPhoneGoal card or mid-sem dateShows the route, runs past-paper practice, reroutes on missesBlue, Yellow
LabLaptop"Open on laptop" from a node, or the lab's QR codeCopilot overlay: points at controls, asks for predictions and "why", runs the debug caseGreen
RevisePhoneA flickering node or a notificationTwo-minute checks with less help and a suggested notch toward EnglishAll four
Teach KikiPhone, by voiceA ring three-quarters full, or the interview goalPlays a confused junior, then gives feedback against a rubricYellow

Interaction rules:

  • The dial is always in the lesson header. The student can drag it any time. Kiki suggests a change with a chip ("3 right in a row. Try one notch more English?"), and the student taps "Yes" or "Not now". Moving toward Odia never costs points. It is recorded as evidence of how much support they need.
  • Kiki is present, not a chat window. Four dots sit in the corner. Tap or hold to talk, in Odia or English. Kiki answers mostly with actions (a diagram, a simpler version, a hint, pointing at a control) rather than long text.
  • The hint ladder. Kiki asks a question first, then gives a nudge, then a worked step, and only then the answer. Each rung used is recorded as evidence.
  • Diagnosis drives the next step. A concept gap sends the student to a prerequisite node ("Rerouting…"). A language gap sends them to word stickers and an easier English version of the same question.
  • Notifications report progress, not guilt. Examples: "Your Diode node is flickering", "2 stops left before mid-sem", "Lab tomorrow: 5-minute warm-up?". There are no streak warnings.
  • Mastery view. Four colour bars per subject, a weekly English-percentage trend, the size of the sticker deck, and milestones such as "First concept without Odia". A weekly card can be shared to WhatsApp, which feeds back into acquisition.

Recommendations on the open questions

Recommended: demo Electronics only, using a "Diodes and rectifiers" chapter that ends in a half-wave rectifier lab inside a browser-based simulator. The other seven answers follow from that choice. Change the status as the team decides.

QuestionRecommendationWhyStatus
Demo one branch or three?One branch: ElectronicsThe lab gives the clearest visual payoff (AC sine wave in, rectified wave out), and the call already named its toolsAgreed
Which chapter and first node?Diodes and rectifiers, about 10 nodes: semiconductor basics, PN junction, forward and reverse bias, V-I characteristic, diode models, half-wave rectifier, full-wave rectifier, filter capacitor, ripple, Zener regulator. First node: the diode as a one-way gate.Builds on Class 12, appears in first-year Basic Electronics syllabi, and matches the architecture's 10-node targetAgreed
Which lab tool?A browser-based lab that looks like a SPICE simulator, with 5 to 10 known screen states. Kiki still reads screenshots with Gemini. Debug case: the diode is placed backwards, so only the negative half-cycles appear. Real LTspice is the next step after the demo.The architecture doc prefers a controlled browser simulation. Nothing to install on college laptops, the demo is reliable, and the draw-your-prediction overlay is easy on our own canvas.Agreed
Is the dial one global setting or set per concept?One global dial. Moving it inside a lesson applies to that lesson, then Kiki asks "Keep this everywhere?"One setting is easy to understand. Differences between concepts appear as Kiki's suggestions, not as extra settings.Agreed
Spoken-English listening check in onboarding?Leave it out. Add listening inside lessons later: Kiki reads an English sentence aloud and the student picks its meaning.Keeps the first minute short. Listening is better measured on real lesson content.Agreed
Syllabus and past-paper upload in the 10-day scope?Yes, narrowly. Upload one real syllabus or past paper; Gemini maps it onto our curated graph and counts topics. If parsing fails, fall back to the curated graph silently.A strong Gemini multimodal moment for judges, kept reliable by the curated graphAgreed
Phone-to-laptop handoff?A QR code on the laptop, scanned by the signed-in phone, like WhatsApp Web. Google sign-in on the laptop as the fallback.Lab laptops are shared, so students should not type passwords on them, and the pattern is already familiarAgreed
What if Kiki is unsure what is on screen?Below a confidence threshold Kiki never guesses: "I can't see clearly. Which screen are you on?" It shows three thumbnails of known states to tap.Pointing at the wrong control destroys trust. A tap costs 2 seconds.Agreed

Measuring impact

The headline we want to show judges: the gap between what students know and what they can say in English gets smaller. We measure concept, English and practical skill separately, as the vision doc asks. None of this has been run yet.

Pilot plan: 10 to 20 Odia-medium first-years. Before the submission if possible, otherwise presented as the planned next step.

MeasureBefore and after the same conceptDimension
Concept scoreThe same question asked in OdiaBlue
English answer scoreThe same question asked in EnglishYellow
Odia-to-English gapThe difference between the two scores above; it should shrinkBlue against Yellow
Handwritten 5-mark answerMarked with Snap your answer (feature 21)Blue, Yellow
Spoken explanationOne 60-second explanation, scored with the same rubricYellow
LabCompletion time and hints usedGreen

Product numbers to track during the pilot: time to the first lesson, session completion, the good-session rate, dial movement toward English over a week, and how many students return after a reminder.

Student journey and data model

Every screen a student sees is now specified, module by module, in Student journey. For each screen it gives what it shows from top to bottom, every button and what it does, and the states it handles. The first page is screen 1.1.

The data model behind it is subject-agnostic and is described in Data model: one pyramid for a chapter, a topic or a single question, and one intake for anything a student brings. The journey tab ends with 11 decisions for the team to confirm, including four bottom tabs (Today, Map, Practice, Me) and one Kiki door for asking and adding anything.

UI 1: Creative direction

The concept is Breadboard: colour is earned. The app looks like a friendly electronics breadboard drawn on graph paper, and Google's four colours appear only as the student earns them. A new student sees a calm, mostly ink-on-paper app with one spot of colour: Kiki's four dots. By mid-sem, their map is lit up in Blue, Red, Yellow and Green.

Why this direction:

  • It makes progress visible without a single number. The screen itself becomes more colourful as the student learns, and a glance at the map is a progress report.
  • It belongs to the subject. Wires, LEDs, current, switches and oscilloscope traces are the native language of Electronics. Loading, success and navigation all borrow from it.
  • It is Google without being a Google clone. The four colours, Material 3 shapes and Material Symbols carry the brand. The breadboard and Kiki make it ours.
  • It is playful, not kiddy. Engineering students already love this imagery. It feels like a smart toy, not a children's app.

The breadboard metaphor, element by element:

UI elementBreadboard meaning
Dotted 8 px background gridThe holes of a breadboard, and graph paper
Concept node on the mapA component plugged into the board
Prerequisite lineA jumper wire
Mastering a conceptPower on: its LED lights up and current flows down the wire
LoadingA pulse of current running along a wire
Error or lost connectionA broken wire, and Kiki's dots drift apart
Lab modeAn oscilloscope screen: dark glass, glowing traces
Recording your EnglishYour voice drawn live as a waveform on a scope

Seven principles every screen follows:

  1. Colour is earned. Brand colour marks progress and Kiki. Everything else is ink and paper.
  2. One decision per screen. One thumb, one main action, on a phone held in one hand.
  3. Two scripts, one voice. Odia and English are set as equals. An English technical term always looks the same, everywhere.
  4. Show, then tell. A picture or an interactive first, words second.
  5. Kiki acts, not chats. Kiki points, draws, highlights and asks short questions. No long chat bubbles.
  6. Light enough for 3G. The first screen loads in under 1 MB. No video in the critical path.
  7. Honest feedback. Rings, counters and celebrations reflect real evidence only.

UI 2: Foundations

Foundations are design tokens in code from day one. Each Google colour has two values: the bright brand hue for fills, LEDs and Kiki, and a darker shade for text and icons so it stays readable on white.

Colour

TokenFillText and icon shadeUsed for
Blue#4285F4#1967D2Concept dimension, primary buttons, the mid-sem route line
Red#EA4335#C5221FWords dimension, stickers, term chips once collected
Yellow#FBBC05#9A5500English dimension, voice and Teach Kiki. Never yellow text on white.
Green#34A853#137333Lab dimension, the lab-mode scope trace
Paper#FBFAF7—App background, a warm white
Ink#1F1F1F—Main text, lines, unlit components
Pencil#5F6368—Secondary text, unlit wires
Grid dot#E3E1DC—Breadboard dots
Scope glass#0E1116—Lab-mode background

Two deliberate rules:

  • Red never means "wrong", because Red means Words. A wrong answer is "not yet": a pencil-grey outline with a gentle shake, never a red X.
  • Green never means "correct", because Green means Lab. A correct answer lights up in the colour of the dimension being practised.

Check the text shades with a contrast checker before shipping.

Type. All fonts are free on Google Fonts. Odia glyphs look smaller than Latin at the same size and need room for vowel marks above and below, so Odia is set 2 px larger with more line height.

RoleLatinOdiaSize and line height (Latin / Odia)
Display, headingsBaloo 2Baloo Bhaina 2 (same family)28/34 · 30/42
BodyNoto SansNoto Sans Oriya16/24 · 18/30
English term chipNoto Sans SemiBold—15/20
Values, units, codeRoboto Mono—14/20

Shape. Material 3 Expressive throughout:

  • Buttons are full pills with a 3 px darker bottom edge, like a keyboard key, that presses down 2 px on tap.
  • Cards use 24 px corners, bottom sheets 28 px, and map nodes are 16 px squircles.

Motion. Springy, never slow.

  • Tap feedback: 120 ms.
  • Small changes: a 250 ms spring.
  • Screen changes: 350 ms.
  • Celebrations: at most 1.2 s.
  • Current flow: a dashed line moving along a wire on a 1.5 s loop.
  • With reduced motion turned on, everything becomes simple fades.

Sound. Only five sounds, all off with one switch:

  1. A soft tap tick.
  2. A sticker pop.
  3. A rising three-note chime for a correct answer.
  4. A low power-on hum when a concept is mastered.
  5. Kiki's voice, which always waits for a tap.

Haptics. Short vibrations on Android:

  • 10 ms on each dial notch.
  • 30 ms on a correct answer.
  • A short pattern when a concept is mastered.

Icons and illustration.

  • Icons are Material Symbols Rounded. Their fill axis animates from outline to solid when something is earned, so icons follow "colour is earned" too.
  • Illustrations are ink line drawings with flat fills, in the spirit of Google Doodles. Circuits are drawn as clean schematics.
  • Kiki is the only character.

UI 4: Standard components and system states

Everything that isn't signature comes from Material 3, restyled with our tokens. Don't design these from scratch.

  • Buttons: filled pill (the tactile key), tonal, text, icon button. One filled button per screen.
  • Chips: choice chips (branch, goal) and filter chips (sticker deck).
  • Bottom sheet: term details, dial explainer, share options. Used instead of dialogs on the phone.
  • Navigation bar: three tabs only: Map, Stickers, Me. Lessons open full screen over it.
  • Snackbar: "Saved", "Rerouting…", "Back online".
  • Linear progress: the segmented four-colour version in the lesson player.
  • Text field: the base of the answer composer.
  • Top app bar: small, holding the dial and close button inside lessons.
  • Switch: sound on or off, reminders.

System states, in the breadboard voice:

StateWhat the student sees
LoadingA pulse of current runs along a wire. Kiki's dots breathe. Skeleton cards keep the layout steady.
OfflineA thin banner: "No signal. Your progress is saved on this phone." Cached lessons and stickers still work.
ErrorA broken-wire illustration, Kiki's dots drift apart, and one action: "Try again". No error codes.
EmptyAn unplugged board with one glowing hole: "Your first component goes here", and a Start button.
Permission (microphone)Kiki explains in Odia why it needs to hear them before the browser asks.
AI is slowKiki says "Thinking…" with the wave animation. After 4 s, a pre-generated fallback appears.

UI 5: Screen inventory

The demo needs 28 screens: 22 on the phone and 6 on the laptop. Four are hero screens that get the most design time, because the judges will remember them. Hero 4 is Snap your answer (screen 23), in the second table.

  • Hero 1: Lesson with the dial (screen 7). The paragraph morphs from Odia to English while the term chips stay put. This is the unique pedagogy in one gesture.
  • Hero 2: Learning receipt (screen 12). Before-and-after, the student's own English voice, and the map lighting up. This is the proof of learning.
  • Hero 3: Lab with Kiki (screen 17). Draw your prediction, then Kiki spotlights the tool and the real waveform overlays the sketch. This is Gemini seeing the screen.

UI 6: How we build it

The full plan is in the Build plan tab: the roadmap with four gates, a 49-task checklist, the demo script, and risks with fallbacks. The tools below are the suggested stack.

The components are built and live in the Breadboard design system: tokens, 21 interactive components with guidelines, and a React-ready bundle (window.Breadboard). Local copy: design-system/project/ in the project folder. Two text shades were darkened there to pass contrast checks: yellow text is #9A5500 and green text #137333.

Suggested tools, for the team to confirm:

NeedToolWhy
App and tokensReact with Tailwind, tokens as CSS variablesFast to build, and tokens stay in one place
Spring motionMotion (formerly Framer Motion)Springs and layout animation built in
KikiPlain SVG circles animated with MotionFour dots need no Lottie or Rive files
Breadboard mapReact Flow, with custom nodes and animated edgesPan, zoom and wires out of the box
Explorable and waveformsHand-written SVGSmall, and fully under our control
Prediction canvasperfect-freehandSmooth finger strokes
IconsMaterial Symbols Rounded, variable fontThe fill axis animates "earned"

Two rules for the whole build:

  • Test on a cheap Android phone from day 3. Check that Odia conjuncts render correctly in our fonts, and check load time on throttled 3G.
  • Every AI moment in the demo has a cached fallback. The live call runs, but the demo never waits more than 4 s.

UI 7: Open questions

Tab 2 · Student journey

Student journey, screen by screen

Oct 11, 2026 · @Arpan

This tab defines every screen a student sees, from the first page to the last repair, for any subject, chapter, topic or single question. Each screen lists what it shows from top to bottom, every button and what it does, the states it must handle, and the data it reads. The diode chapter supplies the example values only; every screen works the same way for a Chemical Engineering topic built from notes or one Mathematics question typed at night.

App map

Every way in leads through one short onboarding into four tabs. Kiki's dots, on every screen, are the single door for anything the student brings, which is what keeps the product general. Lessons, checks, receipts, revision and practicals are full-screen flows that the tabs open; they hide the bottom bar until the student finishes or closes them.

Rules every screen follows

These rules hold on every screen below, so the per-screen specs only list what is different.

The shell. A main screen has a top bar and a bottom bar. Full-screen flows (onboarding, a lesson, a timed paper, the camera, a practical) hide the bottom bar and show a close button instead, so the student is never pulled out by accident.

PartWhat it holdsBehaviour
Top bar, leftCourse switcher: the course title and a down arrow ("Basic Electronics")Opens a sheet listing the student's courses, "My questions" (their self course) and "Add a course"
Top bar, rightKiki's four dotsTap opens Ask Kiki (Module 3). The dots show Kiki's state: idle, thinking, has a suggestion
Bottom barFour tabs: Today, Map, Practice, MeThe current tab is filled in blue ink. Tapping the current tab scrolls it to the top
Teaching screensThe language dial chip, top right beside Kiki ("Dial 3")Opens the dial (Module 5). Shown wherever there is teaching text: lessons, Ask Kiki answers, feedback, marked answers

Navigation rules.

  • Back always returns to where the student came from; it never skips a step they have not seen.
  • Closing a lesson, a paper or a practical mid-way asks once ("Leave the lesson? Your place is saved.") and then saves the exact beat or page.
  • Deep links (smart links, notifications, share cards) open the target screen with Today underneath, so Back lands somewhere sensible.

Kiki. Two forms only: the four dots for presence and the pointer for guidance. Kiki suggests; the student decides. Kiki never moves the dial, never auto-plays sound without the voice setting on, and never blocks a screen with a pop-up. A suggestion appears as one line beside the dots with two buttons: the action, and "Not now".

The language dial. One global setting with five notches: 1 Mostly Odia, 2 Odia with English terms, 3 Half and half, 4 English with Odia help, 5 Exam English. Only the student moves it. Kiki can suggest a notch ("Try one notch more English?"), and every change is recorded as evidence. Technical terms stay in English at every notch, in a term chip.

Colour means a skill. Blue concept, red words, yellow exam English, green lab (or the subject's practical label). Red never means wrong and green never means correct. A subject with no practical work shows three ring segments, not an empty fourth.

Copy. Short, plain sentences in sentence case, no emoji. "Not yet", never "wrong". Grammar and spelling that do not block meaning are never penalised.

Generality. No screen hard-codes a subject. Every label that varies comes from the data:

On screenComes from
Course, chapter and concept names, can-do linesCourse, LessonPlan, Concept
The green dimension's name (Lab, Practical, Drawing, Code) and whether it showsSubjectProfile.practice
Which beats a lesson hasWhat the concept contains: no interactive means no Explore beat; no practical means no Lab tease
Exam countdown and paper formatGoal and ExamProfile; hidden when there is no exam
"From your notes, page 3" tagsSourceRef on each piece of content
"Kiki-made" labelreview.status is auto_checked (not yet checked by a teacher)
Weight badges ("asked in 4 of 5 papers")examSignal; hidden when its basis is none, marked "estimate" when estimated

Three key screens

These are layout wireframes, not visual design; the Breadboard design system supplies the look. The first page asks for one tap. Today leads with one primary card. The Explain beat shows Kiki's pointer marking the phrase it is narrating, in the colour of the skill (red for a technical term), with the dial chip always in reach.

Module 1: First page and onboarding

A new student goes from a link to their first lesson in about 60 seconds: one first page, a promise, up to five short questions, and their route. No sign-up is asked for until they have learned something (Module 8). Every question can be skipped; skipped answers get sensible defaults and can be changed in Me.

Flow: link preview > 1.1 First page > 1.2 Promise > 1.3 Which feels easy > 1.4 About you > 1.5 Goal > 1.6 Plan > 1.7 Before > 1.8 Your route > first lesson.

1.0 Before the app: the link preview

What a classmate sees in WhatsApp before tapping. It is built from the smart link, so it names the real course and chapter.

  • Shows: Kiki's four dots on paper, the title "Learn Diodes and rectifiers in Odia and English", one line "Explained in Odia. Written in exam English. Free.", and the short link.
  • Tap: opens the web app in the phone's browser. No install and no store page. "Add to home screen" is offered only after the first lesson.
  • Generic rule: the title uses the link's most specific target: concept, then chapter, then course. A share card shows the sharer's name and what they just learned.

1.1 The first page

The page that decides whether the student stays. It must load as text first on 3G, explain the product in one breath, and ask for nothing but one tap.

Shows, top to bottom:

  1. Top bar. Empty on the left. "Sign in" as a text button on the right, for students who already have an account.
  2. Context chip, only when the student arrived by a link. A class link reads "ECE 1st year · Basic Electronics · from your class group". A share card reads "Bikash shared: Half-wave rectifier". A direct visit shows no chip.
  3. Kiki arrives. The four dots gather into the pointer, which looks up and waves once (about 1 second, skipped when the phone asks for reduced motion).
  4. Greeting, as a bilingual pair: the Odia line first, the English line under it in a lighter weight: "Hello, I'm Kiki."
  5. The promise, two lines: "Learn any chapter in Odia and English. Then write it in exam English." With a class link, a third line names the chapter: "Your class is on Diodes and rectifiers."
  6. Three proof lines, each with a small coloured mark:
    • Blue: "Ideas explained in Odia, terms kept in English"
    • Yellow: "Your answers marked for the idea and the English separately"
    • Green: "Your syllabus, your notes, your exam" (the subject's practical label is not needed here)
  7. Primary button: "Start", with "About 1 minute to set up" under it.
  8. Secondary button: "I have a question right now".
  9. Footer: "No sign-up needed. Your progress stays on this phone until you save it." Then a "Privacy" link and the app language switch "ଓଡ଼ିଆ | English".

Buttons:

ButtonWhat it does
StartCreates an anonymous learner and goes to 1.2 Promise. Link details (course, chapter, exam date) are carried forward
I have a question right nowOpens Ask Kiki (3.1) straight away. The onboarding questions are asked after the first answer, in two steps: language, then course
Sign inGoogle sign-in sheet. A known account goes straight to Today; an unknown one continues to 1.2 with the account attached
ଓଡ଼ିଆ / English switchChanges the app's own labels (buttons, menus). It does not set the teaching dial; that is 1.3
PrivacyA sheet: what is stored, that photos of answers are deleted after marking unless the student keeps them, and how to delete everything

States:

  • Returning on the same phone with anonymous progress: the greeting becomes "Welcome back", the primary button becomes "Continue" and goes to Today.
  • Slow network: text and buttons render first from the cached shell; Kiki's animation loads last. The page never shows a spinner on its own.
  • Offline on the very first visit: "You're offline. Connect once to get started." with "Try again". After the first visit, the shell and the first lesson are cached.
  • Expired or broken link: the page falls back to the direct-visit version with one line: "That link has expired. You can still start."
  • Link to a single concept (share card): Start skips 1.4 to 1.6 and goes from 1.3 straight to that concept; the skipped questions are asked after its receipt.

Data: reads SmartLink (course, plan, concept, class, exam date). Writes a new Learner (anonymous) with onboarding.arrivedVia.

Sets expectations for the next ten minutes, so the questions feel worth answering.

Module 2: Today

Today is the home tab. It answers one question, "what should I do now?", with one primary card and at most four supporting cards. It is the first screen for every returning student.

Module 3: Ask Kiki or add anything

This is how the product stays general. Whatever a student brings, they bring it through one place: Kiki's composer. They can type a question, say it, snap a homework question, add notes, add a syllabus, a past paper or an experiment sheet. Kiki works out what it is, matches it to what already exists, and only then offers to build something new. Every input becomes a StudyRequest (data model tab).

3.1 Kiki's composer

A bottom sheet that opens from Kiki's dots on any screen, from the Ask bar on Today, or from "I have a question right now" on the first page. It opens half-height and drags up to full.

Shows, top to bottom:

  1. Context line: what Kiki assumes the question is about: "About: Half-wave rectifier" inside a lesson, "In: Basic Electronics" elsewhere. Tap it to change or clear it.
  2. Three suggestion chips that depend on context. In a lesson: "Explain it more simply", "Why 0.7 V?", "Give me an exam question". On Today: "What's on my mid-sem?", "Add my notes", "Quiz me on yesterday".
  3. The thread of this conversation, newest at the bottom.
  4. Input row: a text field reading "Ask in Odia or English", then microphone (hold to talk), camera, attach, and send.
  5. Under the field, when empty: "You can also add notes, a syllabus, a past paper or an experiment sheet."

3.6 Where it lands

A new plan appears on the Map with a "New" marker and joins the route at the place the student chose. Concept-scope plans from questions collect in the course as "Your questions", or in the "My questions" course when there is no course. When a syllabus arrives later, Kiki offers to fold them into the right chapter. Progress carries over, because it is keyed to the concept.

Module 4: Map and route

The Map tab shows where the student is in the course. It has two views of the same data: Route (an ordered to-do list toward the goal) and Map (the breadboard: every concept as a node with its four-colour ring, wired by prerequisites).

4.1 Map tab

Shows, top to bottom:

  1. Shell, with the Map tab selected.
  2. A two-way switch: Route | Map. It remembers the last view.
  3. Route view: the goal header (as on Today), then every stop. Each stop shows its number, title, minutes, weight badge, reason chip and state: done (full ring), in progress (partial ring), next (raised), later. Finished stops collapse under "4 done".
  4. Map view: each lesson plan is one breadboard rail, labelled with its title and progress ("Diodes and rectifiers · 4 of 12"). Broad concepts are clusters on the rail and concepts are nodes. Thin traces show prerequisites.
  5. Filter chips (Map view): All, In my exam, Needs work.
  6. A legend button, bottom right.

Module 5: The lesson player

One concept, in 10 to 15 minutes, as a run of beats. Nothing in a lesson is authored per beat: the player builds the beats from what the concept contains, so a Chemical Engineering concept from notes and a Mathematics concept from a question play exactly like a diode concept.

Which beats a concept gets:

8Try in EnglishAlwaysA short_english or long_written check
9Say itA spoken check exists; otherwise it becomes Teach KikiA spoken check
10Lab teaseThe concept has a practical and the subject has practicalspracticalId

The demo's separate "Kiki explains" and "Learn" beats are now one Explain beat with three modes, because they show the same explanation. Example and Worked question get their own beats because the data model has them for every concept.

5.0 The player shell

Shows: in the top bar, Close (×) on the left, then the progress bar with one segment per beat this concept has, the dial chip and Kiki's dots. In the bottom bar, the primary button (Next, Check or Continue), and "Explain more simply" as a text button wherever teaching text is on screen.

5.1 Hook

Shows: the concept title; a promise card, "By the end you can: explain how a half-wave rectifier works and draw its waveforms"; a teaser question built from the example ("Why does your phone charger need a diode?"); the exam badge ("Asked in 5 of 5 papers", or "estimate"); a source tag when it is from the student's notes; and the minutes.

ButtonWhat it does

I know this alreadyJumps to two quick checks, one concept and one words. Both right: the concept is marked mastered for concept and words, and the lesson continues at Try in English. Otherwise the lesson continues from beat 2, with no penalty

5.2 Explain

Three modes over the same explanation, switched by a segmented control at the top: Kiki explains | Read | Watch (Watch appears only when the concept has a video). It opens in the concept's default mode, and the student's last choice wins after that.

Kiki explains (the walkthrough):

  1. The visual at the top, then the explanation text at the dial notch, with term chips.
  2. For each walkthrough step, Kiki's pointer marks the step's phrase (sweep, marker, lens, connect or circle) in the colour of its skill, while the narration plays.
  3. A caption line at the bottom shows the narration sentence.
  4. Controls: play or pause, previous step, next step, speed (0.75, 1, 1.25), captions on or off, and "Step 2 of 4".

Read:

  1. The visual. Tap it to zoom; it has alt text.
  2. The key idea in a boxed line.
  3. The explanation text at the dial notch, with term chips.
  4. Tapping a sentence toggles it between the current notch and exam English in place. The text is never enlarged.

Watch: narrated slides or the short clip, with captions in the chosen language. With data saver on, it shows the size first ("About 1 MB. Play?").

ButtonWhat it does

Module 6: Checks, hints and diagnosis

Every question in the product, whether in a lesson, a recharge, a practice set or a viva, uses the same question screen and the same feedback. That feedback always judges the idea and the English separately: the core promise.

6.1 The question screen

Shows: the prompt at the dial notch, with English terms in chips and a "Show in exam English" toggle so the student also meets the real wording. Below it is the answer area for the question type. The bottom bar has Check (disabled until there is an answer) and "I'm stuck".

Question typeAnswer area
mcqOption cards; one can be picked
multi_selectOption cards with ticks, and "Pick all that apply"
numericalA number keypad, plus unit chips when the subject marks units. The tolerance is applied silently
term_matchTap a term, then its meaning (or drag)
fill_blankA sentence with a gap; type, or pick from the word bank
order_stepsCards to drag into order
label_diagramLabels to drag onto the visual
short_englishA text box with dictation, sentence starters and the word bank
spokenHold to talk, with the voice scope; the transcript is shown before checking
long_writtenType it, or "Write on paper and snap" (10.10)
diagramA drawing canvas with axes when relevant, or "Snap a sketch"
derivationLine-by-line entry, or snap
predictThe prediction canvas: draw the expected graph or outcome
codeA code box with run and check (after the hackathon)

6.2 Feedback

Shows: a diagnosis card with two lines, each with its own colour mark: Idea (blue) and English (yellow), each reading "ready", "nearly" or "not yet". A third line, Words (red), lists exam terms used and "Exam words to add" when terms are expected. Under the card, the check's explanation. On the student's own answer, Kiki marks what they used: terms swept in red, the core idea marked in blue, exam phrasing underlined in yellow. The colours show skills, never right or wrong.

VerdictKiki says (example)Buttons
Both ready"Idea right. English exam-ready."Next
Language gap"Your idea is right. Now say it the exam way: 'depletion region', not 'empty area'." This counts as evidence for the ideaFix the sentence (rewrite with the suggestion shown), Next
Concept gap"Your English is clear, but the idea isn't there yet. Look at this part again."See why (Kiki points to the phrase in the explanation), Try another
Both not yet"Let's take this slower."Explain again, simpler (one notch towards Odia for this concept), then Try another

The card never says "wrong". A numerical answer with the right value and the wrong unit is a language-style gap: "Right number. The unit is mA, not A."

6.3 The hint ladder

"I'm stuck" climbs one rung per tap. Small dots under the button show how many hints were used. There is no penalty wording.

RungWhat the student gets
1. NudgeA question back: "What does the diode do in the negative half-cycle?"
2. PointerKiki's pointer opens the explanation inline and marks the phrase that holds the answer
3. Worked stepThe first step of the solution, written out
4. Show answerThe answer and its explanation. The check counts as "seen", not as mastery, and a similar check returns in the next recharge

6.4 How the rings move (proposed)

RingEvidence that moves it
Concept (blue)Concept checks; the idea line of English checks; rubric criteria in marked answers; label and sort interactives
Words (red)Term matches; exam terms used correctly in written and spoken answers; Practise 5
Exam English (yellow)English checks, spoken answers, Teach Kiki, and the English rubric in marked answers
Practical (green)Predictions, guided steps, faults found, observations, viva answers. Hidden when the subject has no practical work

Proposed thresholds, to tune in the pilot:

  • A dimension is ready at 0.8, with at least two pieces of evidence.
  • A concept is mastered when every applicable dimension is ready.
  • Review dates follow 2, 5, 12 and 30 days. A concept flickers when its review date passes, and a recharge resets it.
  • Answers given after hints count at half weight.

Five quick items on the weakest or most overdue words, in a mixed format:

Module 8: Learning receipt, share card and saving progress

The end of every lesson proves something changed, then asks for the sign-in only once that proof exists.

8.1 Learning receipt

Shows, top to bottom:

  1. "What changed", with the concept title.

  6. Time spent, and the modes used ("Listened and read").
  7. An honest Kiki line when something did not move: "English didn't move today. Tomorrow's warm-up starts there."

Module 10: Practice

Written exam practice the way the exam is written: on paper. The student snaps the pages, Gemini reads the handwriting and marks each answer against its rubric for the idea, and against the English rubric for language. A repair map then turns the weak spots into short fixes. This is the X factor and the demo's closing moment. The paper format comes from the course's exam profile, so it works for any university pattern.

10.8 Repair map

Weak spots become a short list of fixes, ordered by the marks they can recover.

Shows: a small map of only the concepts this paper touched, with repair badges, and under it the repair items. Each item has:

  • the reason: "You knew the idea but didn't name the depletion region";
  • the fix and its time: "Practise 5 words · 2 min", "2-minute recharge", "Rewrite Q2's opening · 4 min" or "See the worked question · 3 min";
  • its status: to do, done, or re-tested.
ButtonWhat it does
Start fixOpens the fix: a term practice, a recharge, a lesson beat, the worked question or a rewrite
Mark doneFor fixes done off the app
Re-test meA short re-test (10.9); available any time, suggested once all fixes are done
Add to routeAdds the fixes as route stops

10.9 Re-test

One question per repaired spot, through the same flow as 10.2 to 10.6, shortened. The report marks each repair item "Fixed" or "Not yet", and the repair map updates.

10.10 Snap your answer (one question)

The one-question version of the whole loop. It opens from "Try it on paper" in a lesson, from the concept sheet, or from the Quick card.

Flow: the question and marks > write on paper > snap one page > reading > the marked answer (10.7) > a mini repair list of 1 to 3 fixes. It uses the concept's worked-question rubric, or a past question's rubric when one exists.

Module 11: Practicals

One module for every kind of hands-on work: a browser simulation, a physical lab, a software tool, a drawing, coding or field work. The kind and the label come from the practical and the subject profile. The whole module is hidden for subjects with no practical work.

11.1 Practical page

Shows, top to bottom:

  1. The title, with a kind badge: Simulation, Lab, Software, Drawing, Coding or Field.
  2. The linked concepts, each with its ring.
  3. The aim.
  4. Apparatus or tools.
  5. The scheduled date, if known: "Lab on Tue 21 Oct".
  6. "From your experiment sheet", when the class sheet has been added.
  7. The steps count, and the student's progress through them.

Accessibility, everywhere:

  • Every voice line has captions.
  • Every visual has alt text.
  • Tap targets are at least 48 px.
  • Reduced-motion settings stop Kiki's animations.
  • Text can scale to 200% without overlap.
  • Colour is never the only signal: every coloured mark also has a label or an icon.

Tab 3 · Feature journeys

Feature journeys

Oct 11, 2026 · @Arpan

Feature map

The product has 31 features in fourteen groups, and 17 of them are needed for the demo. Feature 21, Snap your answer, is the X factor and closes the demo. Each feature below follows the same template, so it can be built screen by screen:

  • Goal: what the student is trying to do, in their words.
  • Outcome: what the student walks away with, and what the system records.
  • Starts from: every entry point.
  • Steps: what the student does and how the product responds, in order.
  • Edge cases: what can go wrong and what happens then.
  • Done when: the check that says the feature is built.

Every spec is a template that works for any course and chapter. The Electronics chapter "Diodes and rectifiers" is only the worked example used in the demo. Wherever a spec says diode, rectifier or V-I curve, read it as "the current concept, lab or graph".

Getting in

1. Smart links and sharing

Goal: "Open what my friend sent me."

Outcome: The student lands on exactly what was shared, with their class already filled in and no sign-up. The system records the referrer, class code, channel and destination.

Starts from: a WhatsApp message, a class QR code, a lab QR code, or the Share button inside the product.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps Share on a concept, route, sticker or receiptBuilds the card image and a pre-written mixed Odia and English message, then opens the phone's share sheet with WhatsApp first
2Edits the message if they like, picks a group, sendsWhatsApp shows the preview card: Kiki's dots, the title in English with an Odia subtitle, "10 min · Odia + English"
3A classmate taps the linkThe page opens in the browser at under 1 MB, and Kiki's dots appear
4—Reads the destination, class code and referrer. Pre-fills the class and shows "Shared by Rohan · 38 classmates on this route"
5—Continues into First open (feature 2) at that destination
6Scans a QR code with the phone camera or Google LensSame as step 3. A lab QR code opened on a laptop goes to pairing (feature 13)

Edge cases:

  • Unknown or expired class code: they still land on the concept, and the branch is asked later (feature 3).
  • Link opened on a laptop outside a lab: it works, and a small QR code offers "Continue on your phone".
  • Student already signed in: skip First open and go straight to the destination with their progress.
  • Sharer's privacy: show the first name only. Sharers can hide their name in Me.

Done when: a WhatsApp link opens the exact concept with the class pre-filled in under 3 s on throttled 3G, and WhatsApp shows the preview image and title.

2. First open

Goal: "Show me this is worth my time."

Outcome: The student has heard Kiki, knows what the next 10 minutes will give them, has a dial setting, and has answered the "before" question. The system records the starting dial level, the "before" answer and the time to start.

Starts from: any smart link, on a first visit.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps "Tap to hear Kiki"Plays the Odia greeting with captions, naming the sharer
2Reads the promise cardShows the route preview and the can-do sentence. Offers Start, or "Show me the whole map"
3Taps Start, then picks one of three versions in "Which feels easy?"Sets the dial to level 1, 3 or 5 of 5. Kiki points at the dial: "You can change this any time"
4Answers the "before" question, or taps "I don't know yet"Saves the answer for the receipt. Kiki cheers either way
5—Opens the first lesson card (feature 8)

Edge cases:

  • Sound off: captions are always on, and the tap-to-hear step can be skipped.
  • "Show me the whole map": opens the map (feature 5) with the first node glowing and Start still one tap away.
  • Tab closed midway: the state is saved on the device, and returning resumes at the same step.
  • Picked "mostly English" but struggles: Kiki suggests a notch toward Odia later. The dial never moves on its own.

Done when: a student goes from tapping the link to the first lesson card in under 60 s, without typing anything.

3. Setup without a link

Goal: "Make this about my course."

Outcome: The course is set and the first node chosen in a few taps. The system records college, branch, semester and goal.

Starts from: a direct visit, a search result, or a link with no class code.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Hears Kiki and picks in "Which feels easy?"Same as feature 2, steps 1 and 3
2Picks college (search, with nearby colleges first), then branch and semester chipsLoads that course's syllabus. For the demo only Electronics is active, and other branches show "coming soon"
3Picks a goal card: mid-sem, lab, lost in class, or interviewChooses the first node using the rules in the main tab
4Answers the "before" questionOpens the first lesson card
5After the receipt, sees "Make your route exact"Offers syllabus and past-paper upload (feature 7)

Edge cases:

  • College not listed: "Other", type the name, and use the standard syllabus for the branch.
  • Branch not active yet: "Tell me when it's ready" saves their interest, and they can still try the Electronics demo concept.
  • Not sure of semester: default to semester 1.

Done when: a student goes from the first screen to the first lesson card in under 90 s, typing in at most one field.

4. Sign in and saving

Goal: "Don't lose my progress."

Outcome: Progress is tied to a Google account and synced across phone and laptop. The system records the account and merges any progress saved on the device.

Starts from: the Save step of the learning receipt, the Me tab, or laptop pairing when not signed in.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Uses the product without signing inSaves everything on the device automatically, with a small "Saved on this phone" note
2Reaches the receipt's Save step"Sign in with Google to keep your ring and route", then opens Google's one-tap sign-in
3Picks an accountMerges the on-device progress into the account. The ring animates "Saved"
4Comes back another dayRecognises them, skips First open and opens the map at their next stop

Edge cases:

  • Declines: progress stays on the device. Ask again only after the next completed concept, and at most twice.
  • Account already has progress: merge, keeping the stronger evidence for each concept.
  • Shared family phone: "Not you? Switch account" in Me.

Done when: a student who signs in at the receipt sees the same ring on the laptop after pairing.

Finding the way

5. Breadboard map

Goal: "Show me where I am."

Outcome: The student sees every concept in the chapter: which are done, which is next, which are locked, and how they connect. They reach the next step in one tap. The system records which nodes they open.

Starts from: the Map tab (home), the zoom-out at the end of the receipt, or "Show me the whole map".

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Opens the Map tabShows the board of 10 "Diodes and rectifiers" nodes, with Kiki as the pin on the current node, the goal card on top and a big "Continue with Kiki" button
2Taps "Continue with Kiki"Opens the next step the Learning Orchestrator chose: a lesson, a revision or a lab
3Or taps a nodeOpens the node sheet: name in English and Odia, the XS ring with its four segments explained, prerequisites, past-paper weight ("asked in 4 of 5 papers"), linked lab, and Start or Revise
4Taps a locked nodeThe sheet names the prerequisite to finish first, with "Take me there" and "Try anyway"
5Pans and pinchesMoves around the board. Double-tap resets the view

Node states:

  • Locked: grey outline, unplugged.
  • Available: outlined, LED off.
  • In progress: a partly filled ring.
  • Mastered: LED on, with current flowing out to the next nodes.
  • Flickering: the LED dims, meaning it's time to revise.

Edge cases:

  • Small phone: the board becomes a vertical scrolling layout, top to bottom, instead of wide.
  • "Try anyway" on a locked node: allowed, because the choice is the student's. Kiki warns once, and the result counts as normal evidence.
  • More chapters later: a chapter switcher at the top of the map.

Done when: in testing, students can say what their next step is within 5 s of opening the map, and reach any node in two taps.

6. Mid-sem route

Goal: "Tell me what to study, in what order."

Outcome: An ordered list of stops up to the exam date, with an ETA that updates as they learn. The system records the exam date, the route and every reroute.

Starts from: the "Mid-sem is coming" goal, a class route link with the exam date, or the route toggle on the map.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Picks the mid-sem goal, or arrives on a route linkConfirms the exam date (pre-filled by the class code) and asks for daily time: 15, 30 or 60 min
2—Orders the stops by prerequisites, past-paper weight and current mastery. Draws the blue line with pins and an ETA pill: "9 stops · 6 h 40 min · about 30 min a day"
3Taps "Start route" or "Continue"Opens the first stop's lesson
4Finishes a stopThe pin becomes a lit node, the counter drops and the ETA updates
5Answers in a way that shows a concept gapShows a "Rerouting…" toast and redraws the line through the prerequisite: "+1 stop, 6 min"
6Opens the app on exam daySwitches to exam-day revision: five quick checks on the highest-weight nodes. After the exam: "How did it go?", then the route is archived

Edge cases:

  • Not enough time for every stop: Kiki says so honestly: "This route needs 9 hours and you have about 6. Here's the 6-hour version." The lowest-weight stops are marked optional.
  • Missed days: the route is quietly re-planned, with no guilt message.
  • Skips a stop: allowed. The stop stays on the route, marked "skipped".

Done when: the route shows the right order, and a deliberately wrong concept answer causes a visible reroute within 2 s.

7. Syllabus and past-paper upload

Goal: "Use my actual syllabus."

Outcome: The map and route reflect their own college's syllabus and past-paper weights. The system records which syllabus topics mapped to which nodes, and how often each node's topic appears in past papers.

Starts from: "Make your route exact" after the receipt, route settings, or setup.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps "Snap your syllabus or past papers"Opens the camera or file picker. Photos or PDFs, several pages allowed
2Takes the photosChecks for blur on the phone and asks for a retake if a page is unreadable
3UploadsKiki shows "Reading…" with progress while Gemini pulls out the topics and question topics
4Reviews the result"I found 8 topics. 7 match your map." Shown as a checklist they can untick. Unmatched topics are listed as "Not in this demo yet"
5ConfirmsMap nodes get heat badges ("in 4 of 5 papers") and the route reorders. Kiki: "Route updated. Rectifiers moved up."

Edge cases:

  • Handwritten or poor photo: ask for a retake, or offer "Use my branch's syllabus instead".
  • Reading fails or times out: fall back silently to the curated map, with "I'll use the standard syllabus for now."
  • Wrong subject uploaded: "This looks like Maths, not Basic Electronics."
  • Privacy: images are deleted after reading, and the screen says so.

Done when: uploading the demo past paper changes at least one node's heat badge and the route order within 15 s.

Learning a concept

8. Lesson player

Goal: "Help me understand this."

Outcome: The student understands one concept through about six short beats, and Blue fills from the checks inside the lesson. The system records each check answer, time per card, dial level per card, hints used and how they used the explorable.

Starts from: "Continue with Kiki", Start on a node sheet, a route stop, or the end of First open.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Opens a conceptFull-screen player: top bar with close, the dial and a four-colour progress bar. The first card states the can-do goal
2Reads the Hook card and taps NextA picture and Kiki's question in Odia, with audio
3Reads an Explain cardAt most 3 to 5 sentences at the dial level, with term chips and one illustration
4Drags the slider on the explorableCurrent dots move through the circuit and the V-I curve draws live. Kiki highlights the knee: "See? Almost nothing until about 0.7 V."
5Answers a check (multiple choice, or tap on the graph)Right: a chime and Blue grows. Not yet: a grey shake, and the hint ladder starts (feature 18)
6ContinuesThe Learning Orchestrator picks the next card: another explanation, a simpler one, a visual, or more practice. Usually two or three explain-and-check rounds
7—Hands over to Collect (feature 10), Try in English (feature 11), Say it (feature 12) and the lab tease

Edge cases:

  • Leaves mid-lesson: resumes at the same card next time.
  • Swipes back: the previous card is shown and earlier answers are kept.
  • Slow network: the demo concept is fully cached. Elsewhere, skeleton cards show while content loads.
  • Repeated misses: the Orchestrator switches approach (a visual instead of text) or reroutes to a prerequisite.

Done when: the diode lesson runs end to end in about 10 minutes, Blue matches the check results, and closing and reopening resumes at the same card.

9. Language dial

Goal: "Explain it in a way I can follow."

Outcome: The student controls the language mix at every moment and moves toward English by their own choice. The system records the dial level on every card, every change, and every suggestion accepted or declined.

The five notches. English technical terms stay in English at every level:

  1. Odia sentences, with English terms as chips.
  2. Mostly Odia, with short English phrases.
  3. Half Odia, half English.
  4. Mostly English, with Odia for the hardest sentences.
  5. English, with Odia only when a sentence is tapped.

Starts from: "Which feels easy?" (the starting level), the lesson top bar (always visible), or Me (the default).

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Sees the dial in the lesson headerThe knob sits on the current notch
2Drags the knobA haptic tick at each notch and a preview sentence while dragging. On release the paragraph morphs and the term chips stay where they are
3Gets 3 right in a rowA ghost knob appears on the next notch: "Try one notch more English?" Yes moves it. "Not now" hides it for the rest of the lesson
4Misses 2 in a row after moving upKiki offers one notch back: "Let's make this one easier." It never moves the dial itself
5Finishes a lesson after changing the dial"Keep this everywhere?" Yes updates the default

One firm rule: questions in Try in English are always in English, whatever the dial says. Only the instructions around them follow the dial.

Edge cases:

  • A level that isn't generated yet: show the nearest cached level with a light shimmer, then morph when ready.
  • A student who stays at level 1: no penalty. Kiki suggests at most once per lesson.
  • Audio: Kiki's narration follows the dial level too.

Done when: dragging the dial in the diode lesson re-renders the text within 300 ms from cache, with every term chip unchanged and in place.

10. Term chips and word stickers

Goal: "What does this English word mean?"

Outcome: The student knows the meaning, pronunciation and use of each key term, and builds a deck they reuse in English answers. The system records terms seen, tapped, collected and used correctly in English, which is the Red evidence.

Starts from: any term chip in a lesson or question, the Collect beat, or the Stickers tab.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps a term chipA bottom sheet: the English term large, its Odia meaning, pronunciation at slow and normal speed, a mini diagram, an English example sentence with Odia below, and "Seen in: Diode lesson"
2Reaches the Collect beatThree new stickers fly in. Each one plays its pronunciation when tapped
3Drags each term to its picture or meaningRight: the sticker pops into the deck and Red grows. Not yet: it slides back, with a hint
4Writes an answer in Try in EnglishThe sticker tray sits under the answer field. Tapping a sticker inserts the term
5Opens the Stickers tabA deck grid with New, Collected and Owned filters. Tap to flip, or "Practise 5" for a quick game
6Uses a term correctly in English answers twiceThe sticker turns solid: owned

Edge cases:

  • No single Odia word exists: the sheet says so and explains the meaning in an Odia phrase instead of a forced translation.
  • Same term, different meaning across subjects (for example "gain"): the sticker shows the meaning for each subject.
  • Pronunciation: not graded in the demo.

Done when: the three diode stickers can be collected, appear in the answer tray, and turn owned when used correctly.

Proving it in English

11. Try in English and diagnosis

Goal: "Can I answer it the way the exam asks?"

Outcome: The student answers an exam-style English question and learns whether any gap is in the concept or in the English, then gets the right next step. The system records rubric results split into concept and English, which feed Blue and Yellow.

Starts from: the lesson after Collect, route practice in exam mode, or revision.

How diagnosis separates the two gaps: when an English answer is wrong, Kiki offers the same question in Odia. Right in Odia means a language gap. Wrong in Odia too means a concept gap.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Reads an exam-style English questionInstructions follow the dial. Any word can be tapped for a short Odia gloss, which is recorded as support
2Writes an answer: types, taps stickers, or speaks"Help me start" offers a sentence starter, also recorded as support
3SubmitsKiki thinks for at most 4 s while Gemini grades against the rubric, scoring concept and English separately
4a—Both solid: the diagnosis card shows "Concept: yes. English: yes." Blue and Yellow grow, and the lesson moves on
4b—Concept right, English weak: "You understand this. You just need the English words." Shows a model answer with their own correct words highlighted, offers word practice, then an easier English version
4c—Wrong: "Try it in Odia?"
5Answers in OdiaRight: the language-gap path (4b). Wrong: a concept gap. "Rerouting…" to a prerequisite or a fresh explanation
6RetriesGraded on the same rubric, then the matching result card

One grading rule: grammar mistakes that don't block the meaning are never penalised. The rubric grades the idea and the correct technical terms. Grammar gets one gentle tip at most.

Edge cases:

  • Blank or "I don't know": treated gently as a concept gap, and the hint ladder is offered.
  • Answer typed in Odia: accepted as concept evidence, then "Now let's try it in English."
  • Very short answer: Kiki asks "Can you say why?" once.
  • Gemini unsure how to grade: Kiki says it isn't sure and asks a quick multiple-choice follow-up instead of guessing.

Done when: three prepared demo answers (both solid, language gap, concept gap) each produce the right diagnosis card and next step.

12. Say it and Teach Kiki

Goal: "Can I explain it out loud in English?"

Outcome: The student hears themselves explain a concept in English and gets one specific improvement. The system records the transcript and a rubric: key idea present, terms used, clarity. Both feed Yellow. The recording stays on the device unless they share it.

Starts from: the Say it beat in every lesson. Teach Kiki opens when a ring is three-quarters full, or from the interview goal.

Say it:

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Sees the promptA sentence starter ("A diode conducts when…") and the stickers to use
2Holds the mic key, or taps to start and stopThe voice scope draws their voice live, for up to 30 s
3ReleasesPlays it back automatically and shows the transcript, with recognised terms as chips
4Listens to KikiOne praise and one fix: "You used forward bias correctly. Try 'conducts' instead of 'passes'." Then "Try again" or "Keep it"
5Keeps itThe recording is saved for the learning receipt

Teach Kiki:

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Opens Teach KikiKiki plays a confused junior: "I don't get why the diode blocks current backwards. Can you explain?"
2Explains by voiceKiki asks one follow-up: "But what happens at 0.3 V?"
3Answers"Oh! I get it now." Then a feedback card: key ideas covered as a checklist, terms used, and one tip

Edge cases:

  • Mic permission denied: Kiki explains in Odia why it needs to listen, and offers typing instead.
  • Noisy hostel room: if the transcript is unclear, "I couldn't hear that well. Try again, or type it."
  • Shy student: "Skip for now" is always allowed. Yellow just doesn't grow from this beat.
  • Speaks in Odia: accepted as concept evidence, with encouragement to try once in English.

Done when: recording, playback, transcript and the one-fix feedback all work in Chrome on a mid-range Android phone within 5 s of release.

Doing it in the lab

13. Lab copilot

Goal: "Help me get this experiment working."

Outcome: The student builds and runs a half-wave rectifier in the browser lab, predicts the output, compares it with the real result, finds a planted fault and explains the result in English. Green fills. The system records how close the prediction was, which steps were done without help, hints used, time to debug, and the explanation rubric.

Starts from: the lab tease ("Open on laptop"), the lab QR code on the experiment sheet, the lab link on a node sheet, or a reminder before lab day.

The lab runs in eight phases: Pair, Brief, Predict, Build, Run, Explain, Debug, Done.

StepPhaseStudent doesProduct responds
1PairOpens the short address on the lab laptop and scans its QR code with their signed-in phoneThe laptop says "Hi Bikash". The phone shows "Lab connected" and stays as a companion screen
2BriefReads and listensKiki explains the aim at the student's dial level, shows the circuit diagram, and lists the four parts needed
3PredictDraws the expected output over the input sine wave on the prediction canvasSaves the sketch for comparison
4BuildDrags parts from the palette and wires themKiki spotlights the next control ("Pick the diode from here"). On wrong wiring it asks a question instead of fixing it: "Where does current go after the diode?"
5RunPresses RunThe scope shows the output. Kiki overlays the sketch on it: "Close! You missed that the negative half is flat."
6ExplainAnswers in English, typed or spoken: "Why is the negative half missing?"Graded like feature 11, feeding Yellow and Green
7DebugHears "Your lab partner changed something. Find what's wrong." Kiki has planted the fault card that matches their weakest misconception (see Debug challenge below). Demo example: the diode is flipped, so only negative halves appearKiki asks "why" questions, and the hint ladder runs if they get stuck. They fix it and run again
8DoneWatchesGreen fills with the power-on animation. The phone ring turns green at the same moment. A short lab summary (prediction against result, time, hints) goes into the receipt

Edge cases:

  • Kiki unsure of the screen: "I can't see clearly. Which screen are you on?" with three thumbnails of known states.
  • Skips Predict: allowed. Kiki says once, "Guessing first helps you learn."
  • Stuck in Build for more than 2 minutes: Kiki offers a step-by-step mode.
  • Laptop closes or the network drops: the state is saved and the lab resumes at the last phase.
  • No laptop: a simplified phone version of the lab, after the hackathon.

Done when: the full lab, including either of the two demo faults, can be finished in about 8 minutes. Kiki spotlights the right control in each of the 5 to 10 known states, and the phone ring turns green within 2 s of finishing.

Debug challenge, for any course

The planted fault is never hard-coded. Every lab carries a few fault cards, and the Learning Orchestrator plants the one that matches the student's weakest misconception. The puzzle is aimed at that student's own gap. The debug screens are the same in every course: symptom, guess, test, fix, explain.

Seven fault types cover any lab, with examples per branch:

Fault typeElectronicsElectricalChemical
Flipped: direction, sign or orientationDiode reversedTransformer polarity swappedFlow direction reversed
Wrong value: size or unit100 Ω instead of 10 kΩWrong turns ratioGrams entered as kilograms in a mass balance
Missing pieceNo load resistor or groundNeutral not connectedRecycle stream left out
Wrong connectionSeries instead of parallelStar wired as deltaStream sent to the wrong unit
Wrong tool settingSimulation stop time too shortWrong meter rangeWrong solver or unit settings
Wrong measurementProbe on the wrong nodeAmmeter wired in parallelReading the wrong axis
Wrong assumptionIdeal diode used at low voltageLosses ignoredIdeal gas law at high pressure

What a fault card holds:

  • Type: one of the seven above.
  • Target misconception: the concept and misconception it tests.
  • How to plant it: the exact change to the lab state.
  • Visible symptom: what the student will see go wrong.
  • Fixed when: a check on the lab state or the output, within a tolerance.
  • Kiki's "why" questions: three of them, from open to specific.
  • Explanation rubric: how the English explanation of the fix is graded.

Where fault cards come from:

  1. Curated by the team or faculty for the demo labs.
  2. Drafted by Gemini for any new chapter, from the concept's misconceptions and the lab spec or the student's uploaded experiment sheet (feature 20).
  3. Checked by the simulator. Each draft is run, and a card is kept only if its output differs visibly from the correct setup, so there are no unfindable faults.

Demo scope: two fault cards on the rectifier lab. One is Flipped (diode reversed). The other is Wrong tool setting (stop time too short to show a full cycle). Two students with different mistakes get different faults, which shows on stage that it isn't hard-coded.

Honest limit: Kiki's screen reading still covers only the 5 to 10 known states of each lab. We claim the fault design works for any course, not that any course's lab works automatically yet.

Closing and coming back

14. Learning receipt

Goal: "Did I actually learn something?"

Outcome: The student sees evidence of what changed in this session and leaves with one next step. The system records a session summary and whether it was a good session: the can-do goal met in English, at least one ring colour moved, and a next step booked.

Starts from: the end of every lesson, the end of a lab (lab version), or the end of a revision (short version).

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1WatchesBefore and after side by side: "10 minutes ago: I don't know yet. Now: correct, in English."
2ListensReplays their Say it recording: "You said this, in English."
3WatchesThe XL ring fills Blue, Red and Yellow in turn. Green pulses if the lab is still to come
4WatchesZooms out to the map. The node lights up, current flows on, and the route counter drops
5Reads"3 new English words", and the dial change if there was one
6Signs in, or skipsOnly if not yet signed in (feature 4)
7Shares, or skipsThe share card for WhatsApp (feature 1)
8Picks a next stepTwo suggestions, for example "Next stop: Diode as a rectifier, 12 min" and "Remind me before Tuesday's lab"
9Taps DoneKiki's four-colour burst and an Odia goodbye, then back to the map

Versions:

  • Honest version: "Today you found a gap: current and voltage basics. That's what today was for." The ring shows only what the evidence supports.
  • Lab version: prediction against result, debug time and Green filling.
  • Revision version: only the relit node and the next flicker date.

Edge cases:

  • No "before" question in this session: show first try against final try instead.
  • No recording: skip step 2.
  • Left before the end: a mini receipt on the next open: "Last time you…"
  • In a hurry: Skip is always visible, and the whole receipt takes at most 90 s.

Done when: the receipt works out and shows all three good-session checks from real evidence, and finishes within 90 s.

15. Revise

Goal: "Don't let me forget it."

Outcome: Mastered concepts stay mastered, with less help each time, which is the adaptive fade-out from the vision doc. The system records retention checks, the flicker schedule and the dial level used in revision.

Starts from: a flickering node, a notification, "Continue with Kiki" choosing revision, or exam-day mode.

A node starts to flicker after 2, 5, 12 and then 30 days without use. These intervals are a starting point to tune.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps a flickering nodeOffers a "2-minute recharge"
2Answers 3 or 4 quick questionsOne term (Red), one concept (Blue) and one English answer (Yellow), with less help: the dial suggests one notch more English and hints start one rung higher
3Gets them rightThe LED relights, current flows, and the next flicker is scheduled further out
4Misses oneOnly that segment dims. Kiki offers a 3-minute mini lesson on that part

Edge cases:

  • Many nodes flickering at once: Kiki bundles at most three, highest exam weight first, so it never feels like a pile.
  • Exam within 3 days: revision comes before new route stops.

Done when: a mastered node can be set to flicker with a demo time-skip control and relit through a 2-minute check.

16. Reminders and notifications

Goal: "Remind me at the right time."

Outcome: The student comes back at moments that matter, with no guilt. The system records opt-ins, chosen times and which reminders were opened.

Starts from: "Remind me" on the receipt or the lab tease, or Me settings.

Reminder types: lab warm-up the day before, a flickering node, "2 stops left before mid-sem". At most one per day, with quiet hours from 10:30 pm to 7 am. No streak warnings.
