Kiki everywhere

18. Ask Kiki and the hint ladder

Goal: "I'm stuck. Help me."

Outcome: The student gets unstuck with the least help they need, and is never handed the answer first. The system records which hint rung was reached on each question, which lowers the confidence in that mastery, and what they asked.

Starts from: Kiki's dots on any screen (tap or hold), a "not yet" answer (Kiki offers help), or being stuck in the lab.

Ask Kiki (the student starts it):

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps KikiA small sheet with three suggestions for this screen ("Explain this more simply", "Show me a picture", "What does this word mean?"), plus mic and text box
2Or holds Kiki and speaks, in Odia or EnglishKiki's dots become equaliser bars while listening
3—Kiki answers with an action first: a simpler card one notch toward Odia, a diagram, a highlighted term, or pointing at a lab control. Any text is at most two sentences, with audio
4Asks about something outside the chapter"Good question! That's in Transistors, later. Want a one-line answer now?"

Hint ladder (on a question). Each rung takes one tap on "Another hint":

  1. Question back: "What happens to the depletion region in reverse bias?"
  2. Nudge: Kiki points at the relevant part of the diagram or the key term.
  3. Worked step: the first step of the solution.
  4. Answer: the answer with its explanation, followed by a similar question to try alone.

Edge cases:

  • "Just tell me the answer": Kiki explains why it asks first, but the answer is always at most three taps away. Nothing is locked.
  • Kiki isn't confident: it says so and offers a question card to take to the professor: "Ask your professor: …"
  • Off-topic or inappropriate request: a short, polite redirect back to the lesson.
  • Gemini is slow: "Thinking…", then a cached fallback for the demo concept after 4 s.

Done when: on every check in the diode lesson, all four rungs appear in order, and the rung reached shows up in learner state.

Your own material

19. Your notes become lessons

Goal: "Teach me from my professor's notes."

Outcome: The student's own material (slides, notes, handouts, textbook pages) becomes lessons in the dial format, mapped onto their concept map. As the team agreed in the call, the student's material is the first source of truth and our curated content fills the gaps. The system records the sources uploaded, the concepts found, how they map to nodes, and which source each lesson card came from.

Starts from: "Add your notes" on the map or a node sheet, "Make your route exact" after the receipt, or sharing a PDF straight from WhatsApp into the app (possible once it's installed to the home screen).

StepStudent doesProduct responds

2Picks the filesKiki: "Reading 24 pages…". Gemini pulls out topics, definitions, diagrams and worked examples

4Opens a lesson on one of those nodesCards are generated from their notes first and curated content second. Each card has a source tag ("From your notes, page 7") that shows the page snippet when tapped
5Meets a disagreementKiki shows both versions: "Your professor uses 0.6 V. Many books use 0.7 V. Use your professor's in the exam."
6Taps "Compile my mid-sem pack"A route plus a one-page summary per node at their dial level, which they can download

Edge cases:

  • Poor scans or handwriting: a warning on each affected page, and unreadable pages are skipped.
  • Odia-language notes: accepted too.
  • Very large uploads: the first 50 pages are processed and the rest queued.
  • Copyright and privacy: a student's uploads stay private to them. Only material uploaded by faculty is shared with a class.

Done when: uploading the demo professor's 10-page PDF produces source-tagged lesson cards for at least 3 nodes within 60 s, and shows a conflict note for one planted difference.

Goal: "Help me with this exact experiment."

Outcome: Kiki knows the student's actual experiment: aim, circuit, component values, procedure, expected output and readings table. It sets up the lab and fault cards from that. The system records the experiment spec, the concepts it maps to, and the fault cards generated.

Exam and viva practice

21. Snap your answer (the X factor)

Goal: "Will this answer get marks in the exam?"

Outcome: A handwritten exam answer is graded like a university exam, with concept marks and English marks separated and drawn on the student's own handwriting. They see exactly which marks the English cost and how to get them back. The system records concept and English scores per marking criterion (Blue and Yellow evidence) and the student's recurring English errors.

Starts from: "Practise a 5-mark answer" after a lesson, exam practice on the route, a past-paper question on a node sheet, or the Me tab.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Picks a question, or takes Kiki's"Explain the working of a half-wave rectifier with a neat diagram (5 marks)." Shows the marking scheme in plain words: definition 1, diagram 1, working 2, waveform 1. Optional 8-minute exam timer
2Writes the answer on paper, then taps SnapCamera with a page-edge guide. Several pages allowed
3—Checks readability and crops. Gemini reads the handwriting and the diagram
4Sees the resultTheir own photo with marks drawn on it: blue ticks and notes for the concept under each criterion, yellow underlines where the English cost marks. Score: "Concept 4/5 · English cost you 1 mark"
5Taps a yellow underlineAn Odia explanation, the corrected English sentence, and the term sticker if one applies
6Opens "Rewrite"A model answer built from their own content, not a generic one, with the changes highlighted
7Tries again and snaps a second timeAttempt 1 and attempt 2 compared in the receipt

Edge cases:

  • Parts of the handwriting can't be read: those lines are greyed ("couldn't read"), with an option to type them or retake.
  • Diagram missing or partial: the diagram is scored on its own.
  • Answer written in Odia: the concept is graded, and the English version is shown as the model.
  • Uncertain grading: show a range ("3 to 4 marks"), never false precision.
  • Privacy: photos are private and deleted after 30 days unless saved.

Done when: three prepared handwritten demo answers (strong, weak English, weak concept) each get the correct split marks drawn on the photo within 15 s.

22. Viva with Kiki

Goal: "Don't let me freeze in the viva."

Outcome: The student practises an oral exam in English, either a lab viva or an interview, and learns to answer out loud. The system records the questions, answer transcripts, freeze moments (long silences) and rephrases needed. This feeds Yellow and Green.

Starts from: "Practise your viva" at the end of a lab, a node sheet, the interview goal, or a reminder the day before a lab exam.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Picks Lab viva (from the experiment) or Interview (concept questions)Kiki switches to examiner mode, its dots lining up formally
2ListensA spoken English question: "What is the peak inverse voltage of the diode in a half-wave rectifier?"
3Answers by voiceThe voice scope draws the answer live
4Stays silent for 6 sKiki rephrases in simpler English. After another 6 s, it offers the question in Odia, recorded as support
5Continues through 5 questionsDifficulty rises, with follow-ups such as "Why?" based on their answers
6Sees the result cardFor each question: concept right or not, English clarity, freeze moments. The top 3 phrases to practise, and replay for any answer

Viva survival phrases: Kiki also teaches the English phrases that buy time in a real viva, such as "Could you please repeat the question?" and "May I draw it?". Using them counts as a skill, not a weakness.

Edge cases:

  • Noisy room: a typed fallback.
  • Asks for a repeat: always allowed.

Done when: a 5-question rectifier viva runs by voice, with the rephrase and the Odia fallback both working.

More ways to learn

23. Watch mode

Goal: "Just show me. I'm tired of reading."

Outcome: A 60 to 90 second narrated explainer per concept, following the call's "image with audio" idea. Narration is at the student's dial level, and English terms appear on screen as chips while they are spoken. The system records how much was watched, replays and the dial level. Short generated video is used only where motion matters, such as current flow, and is generated in advance.

3Taps a chipPauses and opens the term sheet (feature 10)
4Moves the dial mid-playThe narration switches language mix at the next sentence
5Reaches the endOne check question, which counts as light Blue evidence

Edge cases:

  • Low data: audio and still images only, about 1 MB per concept.
  • No sound: captions carry everything.
  • Downloadable: for offline study (feature 25).

Done when: the diode explainer plays at two dial levels with term chips in sync with the narration.

24. Software tour

Goal: "What is all this on the screen?"

Outcome: A first-timer knows each panel of the lab tool before the experiment starts, which lowers lab anxiety. This is the call's "what each window does" idea. The system records tour completion and which panels were revisited.

Starts from: the first lab visit, the "?" button in the lab, or a lab QR code for a first-timer.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Opens the lab for the first timeKiki: "First time here? 2-minute tour." Skip is always offered
2Follows the spotlightIt moves panel by panel (parts palette, board, wire tool, Run, scope) with each name in English, an Odia explanation and audio
3Does a tiny task on each panel, such as "Drag any part onto the board"Moves on to the next panel when done
4Finishes"You can find this tour again under ?"

For real tools later (MATLAB, Multisim, LTspice), the same tour pattern runs on screenshots of known screens, or as a narrated video.

Done when: the tour covers every panel of the browser lab, each with one tiny task, in under 2 minutes.

25. Offline packs

Goal: "Let me study in the hostel without data."

Outcome: Lessons, stickers and audio for chosen nodes are downloaded, and progress syncs later. The system records packs downloaded and work queued offline.

Starts from: "Download for offline" on a route or a node.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps "Download for offline"Shows the size ("12 MB") and downloads on Wi-Fi by default
2Studies offlineLessons, explorables, stickers and Watch audio all work. English answers are queued: "Kiki will check this when you're online"
3Comes back onlineProgress syncs and the queued results arrive as a notification

Edge cases:

  • Low storage: offers a smaller pack without audio.

Done when: the diode lesson runs in airplane mode, and queued answers are graded on reconnecting.

Teachers and trust

26. Class pulse for teachers

Goal (teacher): "Where is my class stuck, and is it the concept or the English?"

Outcome: For each concept the teacher sees three numbers: mastered, language gap and concept gap. They also see the top misconceptions and a suggested action. Only class totals are shown, in groups of at least 10, and individual students stay private unless they choose to share. This is the scale story for judges, because no existing tool can tell a professor this.

Starts from: the faculty link with the class code, or a weekly email summary.

StepTeacher doesProduct responds
1Opens the class link and signs in with their college Google accountThe class map
2Looks at the mapEach node has a bar split into mastered, language gap and concept gap. Example: "Reverse bias: 62% language gap, 15% concept gap"
3Taps a nodeThe top 3 misconceptions with anonymised example answers, and the most common English stumbling words, such as "depletion" and "bias"
4Picks an action"Send a 5-minute revision to the class" adds a route stop for everyone. "Make 2 bilingual slides for tomorrow's lecture" generates them with Gemini
5Uploads their own notes or slidesThey become the first source of truth for the whole class (feature 19)

Edge cases:

  • Class smaller than 10: the splits are hidden to protect privacy.
  • Individual answers: never shown unless the student shares them.

Done when (demo): a seeded class of 40 synthetic students shows the three-way split on all 10 nodes. A static screen in the pitch is enough.

27. Report a problem and the glossary

Goal: "This Odia explanation is wrong."

Outcome: Mistakes in AI-written content get caught and fixed, and every English term has one approved Odia explanation used everywhere. The system records reports and glossary versions.

Starts from: a long-press on any sentence or term.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Long-presses and taps "Something wrong?"Choices: wrong meaning, bad Odia, wrong science, other. Optional voice note
2Sends itKiki says thanks. The card shows "Reported" and offers the explanation at another dial level meanwhile
3—The report goes to a review queue for the team or faculty. A fix to a glossary term updates every lesson that uses it
4Gets a notification later"Fixed. Your report helps 38 classmates."

The glossary: one approved Odia explanation per English technical term. All content generation uses it, which keeps terms consistent across lessons, as the architecture doc asks.

Edge cases:

  • Spam reports: rate-limited.

Done when: the report flow works end to end, and a glossary edit changes the term sheet everywhere it appears.

Kiki guidance

28. Kiki explains (walkthrough)

Goal: "Explain it to me like a teacher would."

Outcome: The student follows a narrated explanation in which every sentence is tied to a word or a part of the diagram, and can pause, step back or tap any word. The system records steps played, pauses, replays, words opened in the lens (support), and the dial level during narration.

Starts from: the "Kiki explains" card in every lesson (after the Hook), "Explain it again" from the hint ladder, or Watch mode (the same script played as a video).

Kiki has two forms. The four dots stay in the caption bar. The pointer (a cursor with two eyes and the four dots trailing behind it) moves over the content. The student's own finger or cursor is never replaced.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Presses playThe caption bar plays sentence 1 (Odia first, English under it, following the dial). The pointer flies to the word and an underline sweeps under it
2Keeps listeningEach sentence moves the pointer and marks one target (see the table below). The rest of the paragraph dims while a word is marked
3Taps pause, or taps any wordNarration pauses. A tapped word opens in the lens with its Odia meaning and Hear it
4Steps back or forwardReplays that sentence and its mark
5Reaches the end"Got it, next", or "Explain it more simply": one notch toward Odia, with a regenerated script

How Kiki marks a word. Always one target at a time, in the colour of the skill being taught:

MarkLooks likeUsed forColour
SweepAn underline draws itself under the word as Kiki says itFirst mention of a termRed for technical words
MarkerA highlighter stroke behind the word; the rest of the paragraph dims to 40%The one idea of this sentenceRed for terms, blue for ideas
LensThe word is marked and a card opens under it: the word at 28px, its Odia meaning, Hear itA new or hard termRed
ConnectA dashed line from the word to the matching point on the diagram, which pulsesTying a word to the graph or circuitBlue
CircleA hand-drawn loop around the wordExam vocabulary, a word to use exactlyYellow

Text is never enlarged in place, so the paragraph never reflows. Only the lens zooms. In the lab, the same pointer follows the LabGuide pattern: show me once with a ghost drag, wait at the part for the student's turn, tilt and explain after a wrong move, dim everything except the next control and tap it, then ask "why" at the output (feature 13).

Edge cases:

  • Reduced motion: the pointer jumps instead of flying, and marks appear instantly.
  • Sound off: the captions carry everything.
  • Dial changed mid-walkthrough: the captions switch at the next sentence.
  • Generated scripts: Gemini writes the steps as structured JSON. A step whose target isn't in the paragraph is skipped, and a card has at most 8 steps.

Done when: the diode walkthrough plays 6 steps using all five marks in the right colours, and pause, step back and tap-a-word all work.

Practice and repair

29. Exam practice sets

Goal: "Practise the mid-sem the way it's actually written."

Outcome: The student attempts a full set on paper, against the clock, and gets an analysis: marks for each question split into concept and English, the total lost to English, and the weak spots. The system records rubric outcomes per question and concept (Blue and Yellow evidence), time taken and recurring English errors. Handwriting photos stay private.

Starts from: Kiki's prompt on the home map ("Practise for the mid-sem?"), a route milestone, three days before the exam, a reminder, "Practise this topic" on a node sheet, or later a set assigned by a teacher.

When Kiki prompts: after every 3 completed stops, and 5 days and 2 days before the exam. At most once a day, never during a lesson.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Sees Kiki's prompt and taps "Practise for the mid-sem"Offers three sets: Kiki's mock (built from the stops covered and past-paper weights), a past paper from the class (needs feature 7), or a single 5-mark answer (feature 21)
2Starts the timerThe question paper in the university's format: questions, marks, "draw a neat diagram". Each question can be read in Odia on tap; answers are written in English
3Writes on paper, then taps "I've finished writing"The camera opens with a page-edge guide. Each page is checked for readability, and pages can be reordered
4Sends the pagesKiki shows the marking steps: reading the handwriting, matching answers to questions, marking the concept, marking the English. Gemini reads the handwriting and diagrams and marks each answer against its rubric
5Reads the analysisThe score, a bar split into earned, lost to English and lost to concept gaps, a row per question with its own split, and "Fix these before the exam"
6Taps a questionThat answer marked up on the photo (feature 21): blue for concept, yellow where English cost marks, an Odia explanation and an exam-ready rewrite
7Taps "Make my repair map"Builds the repair map (feature 30)

Marking rules are the same as feature 11. Grammar that doesn't block the meaning costs nothing. A wrong technical word counts as English cost. An unattempted question counts as a concept gap unless the student marks it "skipped for time". When Gemini is unsure, it shows a mark range.

Edge cases:

  • Missing question numbers: Kiki asks the student to match each answer to its question.
  • Unreadable page: retake that page only.
  • Answer written in Odia: the concept is marked, and the English version is shown as the model.
  • Over time: it is marked anyway, and the time is shown.

Done when: the three demo handwriting pages for the 5-question mock produce the 17/25 analysis (3 marks lost to English, 5 to concept) within 20 s.

30. Repair map

Goal: "Tell me exactly what to fix before the exam."

Outcome: A short, separate map of the weak spots from one practice set, ordered by the marks they can win back, each with its own fix and a re-test at the end. Passing the re-test lights those stops on the main map. The system records repair items, fixes done and the re-test result, and updates the evidence.

Starts from: "Make my repair map" on the analysis, a "4 repairs left" card on the home map, or a reminder.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Taps "Make my repair map"Each weak spot becomes a dashed repair node, ordered by marks lost. A concept gap pulls in its prerequisite when the evidence says it is missing
2Reads the mapEach node shows the gap type (Concept or English), the marks lost, the minutes needed and the fix. Total time and the exam date are on top
3Taps "Start repair"Fixes run in order, with Kiki's pointer as the pin. Concept gap: a short Kiki explains plus an explore and a check. English gap: a words drill, then rewriting their own answer in exam English. Missing diagram: draw it along with Kiki. One wrong word: a 2-minute drill
4Takes the re-test4 new questions on the same concepts, written and snapped, or typed if time is short
5PassesThe repair nodes light up on the main map and the wires reconnect. If not passed, a node stays with a smaller fix

Edge cases:

  • More than 6 weak spots: show the top 5 by marks and list the rest as "later".
  • Exam within 2 days: only the English fixes and the biggest concept gap.
  • A second practice set: its repairs merge into the same map, and duplicates combine.

Done when: from the demo analysis, the repair map shows 4 fixes in order of marks lost, each with its minutes, and a re-test node.

Bringing anything

31. Ask Kiki or add anything

Goal: "Here's my question, my notes, my syllabus. Teach me from it."

Outcome: Whatever the student brings goes through one door: a typed or spoken question, a homework photo, notes, a syllabus, a past paper or an experiment sheet. It is matched to what already exists first, so there are no duplicates. Anything new becomes validated lessons at the right scope (one idea, a topic or a chapter), with page-level source tags. This feature replaces separate upload entry points for features 7, 19 and 20, and is the front door of feature 18. The full screen-by-screen spec is Module 3 of the Student journey tab.

Starts from: Kiki's dots on any screen, the Ask bar on Today, or "I have a question right now" on the first page.

StepStudent doesProduct responds
1Types, says, snaps or attaches somethingKiki reads it and states what it found: "6 pages of notes on material balances"
2Waits a few secondsKiki matches it to existing concepts. A question about something known gets a short answer and "Open the lesson". Notes on known concepts are attached as sources
3Sees a proposed outline for anything newScope badge, broad concepts and concepts, "You have this" marks, out-of-scope list, minutes
4Edits or approves the outlineGeneration starts in route order; the first lesson is ready in about a minute, labelled Kiki-made
5Starts the first lesson, or leavesThe rest finish in the background, with a notification; the new plan appears on the Map and in the route

Edge cases:

  • Blurry or dark pages: Kiki asks for a retake of only those pages.
  • Something that is not study material: Kiki says so and offers to answer a question instead.
  • A homework question: hints first, and the full worked answer after one attempt.
  • An outline larger than 5 broad concepts: Kiki proposes two chapters.
  • A syllabus arriving later: concept-scope plans from questions fold into their chapter, and progress carries over.

Done when: in testing, a typed Mathematics question, 6 pages of Chemical Engineering notes and an Electronics syllabus each end in a playable, validated lesson without a single subject-specific screen; the same question asked twice opens the same concept.

Workstreams and scope rules

Five rules that keep 27 features possible in 8 days:

  1. One demo path, end to end, first. A thin version of every demo screen exists by Gate 1 before any one screen is polished.
  2. Cache first, then make it live. Every AI moment ships with cached output by Gate 1, goes live by Gate 2, and falls back to the cache after 4 s.
  3. Build only from the UI kit. A new component is added to the kit before it appears on a screen.
  4. Feature freeze at Gate 3. After Day 8, only fixes and polish.
  5. Test on a real mid-range Android phone every day, on throttled 3G.

If there's time after Gate 3, P1 features are added in this order. Cut from the bottom:

  1. Sign in with Google (4), which is cheap with Firebase Auth.
  2. Mid-sem route (6).
  3. Viva with Kiki (22).

The other features stay as specs in Feature journeys for the pitch's "what's next".

Tab 5 · Data model

Data model

Oct 11, 2026 · @Arpan

The data model is subject-agnostic. One lesson pyramid holds a full chapter, a topic or a single concept, for any subject, built from a syllabus, a professor's notes or one typed question. Subject rules live in one place (the subject profile). Every input becomes a study request that is matched against existing content before anything is generated. Learner, practice and repair data all key to the same concept ids. Three worked ledgers in three subjects pass the validator and type-check: Electronics (a chapter), Chemical Engineering (a topic, from notes) and Mathematics (one question).

Any subject, any scope

ScopeShapeTypical sourceWorked example
Chapter2 to 5 broad concepts, each with 2 to 5 conceptsA syllabus or a class linkDiodes and rectifiers: 4 broad concepts, 12 concepts
Topic1 broad concept with 2 to 5 conceptsNotes, or a chapter nameMaterial balances on steady, non-reacting processes: 2 concepts
Concept1 broad concept with 1 conceptOne questionEigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrix

The student never sees the scope as a difference: every scope plays through the same map, lesson player and practice. When the syllabus arrives, a concept-scope plan made from a question is folded into its chapter (mergedIntoId). Progress carries over because it is keyed by concept.

The whole model

Content is a pyramid with the concept at its centre. Intake turns anything a student sends into a request, matches it to existing concepts first, and only then generates a new or bigger plan. Every learner record (rings, attempts, marked answers, repairs, receipts) keys to the concept id, so a concept made from a question keeps its progress when it later joins a chapter.

What changed from the diode-only version

Diode-only assumptionNow
Branch is one of Electronics, Electrical, Chemicaldiscipline is free text, and subjectProfileId picks the rules. A new subject is a new profile, not new code
Odia is the only student languageA language policy: one source language, any number of support languages, each reviewed per concept
Every plan is a full chapter with a syllabusThree scopes. A plan with no syllabus names the request that sets its boundary
The lab is a circuit simulatorA practical has a kind (simulation, physical lab, software, drawing, coding, field, calculation) with steps, observations, fault cards and viva prompts. Subjects with no practical work hide the green ring
Diagrams are electronics kinds; the explorable is diode-onlyOpen visual kinds with per-subject suggestions; six generic interactive kinds (parameter sweep, step through, label parts, sort steps, compare toggle, simulation)
Exam weight is typed by handThe exam signal is computed from past questions mapped to concepts; its basis says real, estimated or none
Terms and prerequisites stay inside one chapterTerms are unique across the course (borrowed terms are listed); prerequisites cross plans; school topics are bridge nodes
Source only at chapter level; no review stateA source on every explanation, visual, example, worked question and check; a review status (draft, auto-checked as "Kiki-made", teacher-checked, flagged)
No learner, practice or repair dataLearner, goals, route, concept state, attempts with diagnosis, practice sets, marked answers, repair plans, receipts, word stickers, practical runs, classes

Three worked ledgers

LedgerSubjectScopeCame fromWhat it proves
Diodes and rectifiersElectronicsChapter, 12 conceptsCurated (migrated from v1)A simulation practical with three fault cards, two parameter sweeps, a bridge to a Class 12 topic
Material balances on steady, non-reacting processesChemical EngineeringTopic, 2 conceptsA professor's notes, with page-level sourcesA physical lab, a sort-steps interactive, exam signal computed from two sample past papers
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrixEngineering MathematicsConcept, 1 conceptOne typed question in a self courseNo practical (three rings), no syllabus (bounded by the request), a step-through interactive

How anything a student brings becomes lessons

  1. Request. Any input (a question, notes, a syllabus, a past paper, an experiment sheet, a homework photo) becomes a StudyRequest with its pages.
  2. Match first. Existing concepts are found by canonical key and meaning, so a question about ripple opens the existing concept instead of making a duplicate.
  3. Resolve. Kiki picks one action: open existing, answer only, attach the material to existing concepts, extend a plan, or make a new plan at the right scope.
  4. Propose. For anything new, the student sees an outline and confirms or edits it.
  5. Generate. Outline, validate, draft, validate, localize. The first concept is ready in about a minute, while the rest finish.
  6. Label. The content shows a "Kiki-made" label until a teacher checks it. A student's report flags it.
  7. Absorb. Later uploads enrich or merge plans; learner state follows the concept ids.

What every concept contains

Each concept is one node on the student's map and one lesson of 10 to 15 minutes. The course's source language (usually English) is the source of truth. Support-language text (Odia first) and the five dial levels are generated from it and reviewed before they ship. Which parts appear in a lesson depends only on what the concept has.

PartWhat it isShown as
ExplanationA one-sentence key idea and a 60 to 140 word explanationText + image (always, with a visual brief of any kind: circuit, process flow, graph, equation, annotated notes), voice (a Kiki walkthrough of 3 to 8 steps, each tied to a word in the text), and optionally video (narrated slides, or a 20-second generated clip where motion matters), and optionally an interactive (parameter sweep, step through, label parts, sort steps, compare toggle or simulation)
ExampleA concrete scenario and what it provesA card after the explanation; real circuits and numbers where possible
Worked questionAn exam-style question answered in full, line by line, with a rubric that adds up to its marksThe model answer the student learns to write; also the marking scheme for Snap your answer and practice sets
Check questionsAt least 3 questions that test whether the concept is clearAlways a concept check (MCQ, numerical or diagram), a words check (term match) and an English check (short answer, spoken or written), plus a practical check when the concept has a practical. The mix comes from the subject profile

Each concept also records its objectives, prerequisites, the terms it introduces, common misconceptions (these feed diagnosis and the lab fault cards), its exam signal (computed from past papers when there are any), its estimated minutes, where each part came from, and its review status.

How MECE is enforced

Mutual exclusivity and exhaustiveness are checked by a script (data-model/validate.js), not by eye. Every edit to a ledger is validated before it ships.

RuleWhat it checks
Subject and courseThe subject profile is embedded and matches the course; the language policy and dial labels are complete
Pyramid shapeThe shape for the plan's scope (chapter, topic or concept); exactly one parent per concept; every split states its dimension and rationale
Mutually exclusiveEach objective is owned once; each term is introduced once across the whole course; no duplicate objectives, titles, canonical keys, terms or ids
Collectively exhaustiveThe objective tree mirrors the pyramid; every syllabus line is covered, or the plan names the request that bounds it; out-of-scope topics are named
Complete conceptsA visual; a walkthrough whose targets are in the text; a valid interactive (its formulas are evaluated); an example; a worked question with a known type and a rubric that adds up; the subject's check mix; sources and a review status
PracticalsLinked both ways; steps, an expected result, fault cards and viva prompts; none in subjects without practical work
Learning orderPrerequisites exist and form no cycles; no term is used before the concept that introduces it is a prerequisite
Exam signalMatches the past papers when there are any
Across ledgersIn one course: no term introduced twice, no dangling prerequisites or term uses, no duplicate concepts

A test seeds 13 known errors, one per rule family, into copies of the three ledgers. The validator catches all 13 (tools/test-validator.js).

Worked example: Diodes and rectifiers

Each split uses one stated dimension, so siblings never overlap. The chapter follows the AC-to-DC power supply: the diode, then rectify, filter, regulate. A linear supply is exactly these four stages, so nothing in the chapter is left out. Out of scope, named in the ledger: transistors, clippers and clampers, switched-mode supplies, and special diodes other than the Zener.

The new validator found four content issues in this ledger, now fixed in the migration:

  • "Peak inverse voltage" was used by C-2.2 and C-2.3 before C-2.4 introduced it. It now belongs to C-2.2.
  • "Reverse saturation current" was explained in C-1.2 but owned by C-1.3. It now belongs to C-1.2.
  • C-2.3's worked answer needed "centre-tap transformer" without linking it.
  • One 2-mark written check had no rubric.

Files, storage and adding content

All files are in data-model/ in the project folder:

  • types/content.ts, types/intake.ts, types/learner.ts: the types for content (course to check question, practicals, exam profiles, past papers), intake (requests, source documents, outline proposals, generation jobs, smart links) and learners (state, attempts, practice, marking, repair, receipts, classes).
  • subject-profiles.json: the subject rules (Electronics, Electrical, Chemical Engineering, Mathematics, and a generic profile).
  • ledgers/: the three worked ledgers.
  • validate.js: run node validate.js ledgers for every ledger plus the cross-ledger checks.
  • tools/test-validator.js (the 13 seeded errors) and tools/migrate-v1-to-v2.js.
  • archive-v1/: the original diode-only types, ledger and validator, unchanged.
  • README.md: the same rules, for engineers.

Storage: Firestore.

  • Content uses one collection per entity, keyed by id. A concept's explanation, example, worked question and checks sit inside the concept document.
  • Generated text variants live in variants/{entityId}:{field}:{lang}:{level}.
  • Intake uses requests, sourceDocs, jobs and smartLinks.
  • Learner data sits under learners/{id}/ (concept states, attempts, routes, practice sets, submissions, repair plans, receipts, stickers, practical runs).
  • Classes keep only aggregates in classPulse.

Adding a subject: add one profile to subject-profiles.json, with the practical label and kinds, visual kinds, check mix, and whether units matter. No code changes.

Adding a curated chapter or topic (student uploads follow the pipeline above):

  1. Write the governing question, choose the scope, pick one split dimension and name what is out of scope.
  2. Split into broad concepts and concepts, with one objective per node and a canonical key per concept.
  3. Map every syllabus line to concepts, or name the request that bounds the plan.
  4. Have Gemini draft each concept in the ledger shape, from the student's notes first and curated sources second, with a source on every part.
  5. Add past papers so exam signals are computed, not estimated.
  6. Run the validator and fix every error. Have a teacher check the worked answers (review status: teacher-checked).
  7. Generate the support-language text at each dial level, then get a native-speaker review.
